Pottage
POT-tij
noun
From the Old French potage, that which is put into the pot; hence a thick boiled dish of pulse or herbs, the plainest hot food of the poor man’s kitchen — and the price at which a birthright was once sold.

Biblical Definition

Pottage is a thick boiled mess of lentiles, beans, or herbs, seethed in the common pot — the cheapest hot dish the ancient kitchen could set down. Its fame in Scripture is not culinary but moral. Jacob sod pottage; Esau came in from the field faint, saw the red mess steaming, and cried, “Feed me, I pray thee, with that same red pottage; for I am faint” (Gen 25:30). Jacob named his price, and Esau sold his birthright — the double portion, the headship of the house, and the covenant line running down from Abraham toward Christ — for one hot dinner. The Holy Ghost records the transaction with a merciless plainness: “he did eat and drink, and rose up, and went his way: thus Esau despised his birthright” (Gen 25:34). He did not agonize over it; he ate and walked off. Hebrews fixes the verdict for the church: he was a profane person, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright, and afterward found no place of repentance though he sought it carefully with tears (Heb 12:16-17). The word appears again on Elisha’s table at Gilgal, where a great pot of pottage was poisoned by wild gourds gathered in ignorance, and the sons of the prophets cried, “there is death in the pot” (2Ki 4:40) — until the prophet cast in meal and healed it, a small parable of the word of God sweetening a poisoned inheritance.

Webster 1828 Definition

A thick boiled dish of pulse or herbs; proverbially, the trifling price for which Esau sold his birthright.

POTTAGE, a species of food composed of meat, pulse, or herbs boiled together and softened by heat; broth; soup.

From the French potage, from pot, the vessel in which it is seethed.

The pottage of lentiles for which Esau sold his birthright (Gen 25:34).

A common dish of the poor, and of the schools of the prophets (2Ki 4:38).

Proverbially, any small and present gratification bought at a ruinous price.

Key Scripture

Gen 25:29 — "And Jacob sod pottage: and Esau came from the field, and he was faint:"

Gen 25:30 — "And Esau said to Jacob, Feed me, I pray thee, with that same red pottage; for I am faint: therefore was his name called Edom."

Gen 25:34 — "Then Jacob gave Esau bread and pottage of lentiles; and he did eat and drink, and rose up, and went his way: thus Esau despised his birthright."

2Ki 4:40 — "So they poured out for the men to eat. And it came to pass, as they were eating of the pottage, that they cried out, and said, O thou man of God, there is death in the pot. And they could not eat thereof."

Modern Corruption

Esau’s bargain is retold as a sympathetic hunger story rather than as profanity — and the appetite-driven trade of covenant privilege for present comfort goes on unnamed.

expand to see more

The live corruption is the softening of Esau. He is pitied: he was faint, he had been in the field, he thought he was at the point to die, and the birthright was only a legal abstraction anyway — while Jacob was the schemer who took advantage of a starving brother. Scripture will not have it. Jacob’s dealing is nowhere commended, but the inspired verdict falls on Esau alone and it is one word: despised. He was not dying; he rose up and went his way. What he did was to weigh the covenant of God against a bowl of lentiles and judge the lentiles worth more, because the lentiles were hot and now and the covenant was distant and promised. Hebrews therefore calls him a profane person — not a scandalous sinner but a secular one, a man for whom nothing was holy because nothing unseen was real. That is the sin the modern heart commits daily and refuses to name: the marriage traded for an appetite, the Lord’s day traded for a livelihood, the child’s catechism traded for the travel league, the conscience traded for the promotion. Every one of them is Esau’s arithmetic, and every one of them looks reasonable while the pot is still steaming.

Recover the birthright’s worth by looking at what came after. Esau got his dinner and kept it about an hour; he lost a place in the line that ran to Bethlehem. And when he came at last, with a great and exceeding bitter cry, to seek the blessing, he found no place of repentance though he sought it carefully with tears (Heb 12:17) — the tears of a man who wanted the loss reversed, not the sin forgiven. Let the believer read his own bargains by that light. Nothing sold for pottage is ever sold at the price the seller thought. Set against it the mercy of the pot at Gilgal: there was death in the dish, and the man of God cast in meal, and there was no harm in the pot (2Ki 4:41). What Esau despised, Christ purchased and gives freely to those born not of blood nor of the will of the flesh, but of God — and He is the meal cast into an inheritance we had already poisoned.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

A boiled dish of pulse; the byword for a trifling present gain bought with an eternal loss.

expand to see more

Pottage — Old French potage, from pot; that which is boiled in the pot.

Hebrew nazid, a boiled dish, from zid, to seethe or boil up (Gen 25:29; 2Ki 4:38).

The pottage of Gen 25 was of lentiles, and red — whence Esau’s name Edom.

Heb 12:16 renders the price “one morsel of meat” and names Esau profane.

At Gilgal the pottage was death until healed by meal cast in (2Ki 4:40-41).

Usage

"Esau did not agonize over the sale — he ate, rose up, and went his way."

"The birthright was covenant, headship, and double portion; the price was one hot dish."

"There is death in the pot until the man of God casts in the meal."
